one_liner: Lexer generator emitting inline jump-based state machines for 12 languages; beats Ragel on real-world grammars, loses on synthetic repetition.
what_it_does: re2c compiles regex rules embedded in C, C++, Go, Rust, D, Java, JS, OCaml, Python, Swift, V, or Zig source into a function body implementing the lexer, and leaves buffer/driver code to the programmer. There is no fixed runtime template: the generated code calls user-supplied API primitives (buffer cursor, limit, refill), so it plugs into any I/O model rather than assuming one. It also supports POSIX-capture/submatch extraction via the --tags flag, the mode used in its own Ragel comparison.
how_it_is_fast: Instead of Ragel's/Flex's table-driven DFA interpretation, re2c encodes the automaton directly as conditional jumps and character-range comparisons in the target language, letting the downstream compiler apply ordinary branch and jump-table optimizations to the lexer body. It runs its own passes (state merging, jump threading, range-comparison compression) before emitting code, and for --tags submatch extraction tracks minimal per-tag position updates rather than replaying full match history.
when_to_use: Target is C, C++, Go, Rust, D, Java, JS, OCaml, Python, Swift, V, or Zig and you need only a lexer, integrated by hand, not a full parser toolkit
Real-world text formats close to the benchmarked ones (HTTP headers, URIs, log lines, datetimes, email addresses), where re2c ran ~1.0-1.44x faster than Ragel
You're willing to write buffer/driver code yourself in exchange for not depending on Ragel's runtime conventions
Submatch/capture extraction is needed alongside tokenizing (--tags)
Public-domain licensing (no attribution or patent clause) is acceptable or preferred
when_not_to_use: Grammar is dominated by fixed-length repetition/counting patterns (the rep-*/rep-alt-* benchmarks) — Ragel was 1.5-4.1x faster there
You want one tool for both lexing and parsing; re2c only generates the lexer, so you still need a separate parser
You need re2c benchmarked against Flex, Bison, ANTLR, or Boost.Spirit before deciding — its own suite only compares to Ragel
Grammar is large/complex enough that inline-jump code generation risks a much bigger generated file than a table-driven approach (see issue #427, "Generated file too large")
Betting specifically on the Go backend (re2go) for throughput — issue #487 reports a real-world case where generated Go code was reportedly an order of magnitude slower than Go's standard regexp

integration.dependencies: none at runtime — output is plain source in the target language; building the re2c tool itself needs a C++11 compiler and Python 3 (CMake or Autotools)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 to build the re2c tool; whatever toolchain compiles the generated target-language code (e.g. GCC-14/Clang-19 in the benchmarked build)
integration.platforms: any — Linux, macOS, Windows (CMake presets and Mingw cross-compile documented in BUILD.md)
integration.thread_safety: not documented for the tool (single-shot code generator, not a runtime library); generated lexers carry no built-in global state since the caller supplies all API primitives (cursor/limit/refill), so thread-safety is determined entirely by the surrounding driver code
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — explain: like Ragel, re2c requires hand-written interface/driver code around the generated state machine rather than a fixed API, so switching from Ragel means rewriting the grammar in re2c's own regex syntax, not a mechanical swap

gotchas: Nothing runs out of the box: you must define the API primitives (buffer cursor, limit, refill callback, etc.) yourself before generated code compiles or runs correctly — re2c does not validate these definitions
Inline-jump codegen can make generated files much larger than table-driven output for big/complex grammars (issue #427)
The Go backend (re2go) has at least one reported case of being far slower than Go's stdlib regexp on real-world input (issue #487) — don't assume the C/C++ numbers here transfer to other backends

License is a bespoke public-domain dedication with no explicit patent grant; GitHub's license detector reports it as NOASSERTION, which some legal reviews flag despite it being effectively public domain
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick re2c over the catalogued siblings when you need a lexer only (not a full parser) and want one grammar to retarget across many languages (C/C++/Go/Rust/Java/etc.); the siblings (flap, PAPAGENO, Pika Parser, winnow, chumsky, lexy, MPL/FastParse) are single-language parser or parsing-combinator libraries benchmarked against Bison/Flex, ANTLR4, or nom, and none of them compare to Ragel the way re2c does.
verified_claims_summary: On 35 Google Benchmark CPU-time lexer benchmarks (HTTP, URI, Apache log, datetime, email, IPv4, plus synthetic alt/cat/rep patterns), built with GCC-14.2.0 and Clang-19.1.4 at -O3 on an Intel Core i7-8750H, re2c --tags lexers ran roughly 1.0-1.44x faster than Ragel 7.0.4's -G2 simple variant on the real-world formats, but 1.5-4.1x slower on synthetic repetition-heavy patterns — I confirmed the raw cpu_time values (e.g. http-rfc7230-gcc_re2c-simple = 21.17) directly in results_20250131.json.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit 2026-09-17, ~1.3k stars); public-domain dedication makes it freely copyable, though GitHub flags the license NOASSERTION since it's a bespoke dedication rather than a formal OSI license with a patent grant.
